3. The facts which led to filing of this appeal can be narrated in brief as under :
It is the case of the prosecution before the Trial Court that the victim aged 5 years was residing in the area, where accused used to stay.
Both families had well acquaintance with each other.
On 22 nd November 2016, victim told the informant/mother that there is pain in her private part and asked her to apply some medicine.

When she enquired with the victim, she came to know that on 21st November 2016 at about 2.30 pm when the victim had gone to the house of her paternal aunt, while returning, the accused caught her and pulled her to one abandoned place i.e. Wada.
The victim claimed that the accused person moved his hand on her private part and also inserted his finger into the vagina.
It was also told by the accused not to disclose this incident to anyone.
When the accused was confronted with the said fact, he could not answer properly.
However, when the victim was brought before him, he admitted his guilt and assured that he would not repeat such incident in future.

The omissions/contradictions as sought to be pointed out from the testimony of this witness, are not material in order to discard her evidence or to affect the case of the prosecution adversely.
It was the defense of the accused before the Trial Court that owing to the dispute with regard to the house which was to be constructed by the accused, he is falsely implicated.
Unlike, the offences under the IPC, POCSO makes provision of presumptions under Section 29 of the Act.
Thus, once the fundamental facts are proved and established by the prosecution, the presumption of the offence under Act being committed by the accused would come in play.
In such circumstances, the burden would be on the accused to rebut the said presumptions.
Here in this case, the accused has not brought any evidence on record in order to rebut the said presumptions.

Having regard to the aforestated facts, this Court finds no reason or justification to cause interference in the judgment of conviction of the accused for the offences punishable under Sections 363 and 376(2)(j) of the IPC and Section 6 of the POCSO Act.

9. This contention is opposed by learned counsel for respondent No.2 as well as learned APP citing the seriousness of the crime.
It is their contention that the Trial Court has recorded adequate findings and reasons for imposing the sentence of 20 years and, therefore, the same does not deserve any interference.
10. At the relevant time, the minimum sentence of imprisonment for offence punishable under Section 6 of the POCSO was 10 years of rigorous imprisonment.
While imposing punishment, the Court is required to take into consideration various factors such as age of the accused, his responsibilities and his criminal background.
11. Here in this case, the appellant/accused has no criminal history.
